 Blog Post · November 4, 2026
 Why Is California’s Ballot Count So Slow?
 Eric McGhee 
 Subscribe to our blog →
 Eric McGhee 
 Eric McGhee 
 Election Day wasn’t a singular event in California, but the end of a month-long opportunity for voters to cast their ballots. It also marked the start of weeks of ballot counting, a process that has become frustrating for some and even scandalous to others. What are the steps in California’s process, and why does it take so long?
 California is an all vote-by-mail state, which means every voter receives a ballot in the mail by default. Those ballots are sent out no later than 29 days before Election Day. At any time up to and including Election Day itself, voters can return the ballots directly to elections officials through drop boxes, staffed voting sites, or the mail. If mailed back by Election Day, the ballots can arrive up to seven days after and still be counted. The counties then have 30 days from Election Day (which is December 3 this time) to count all ballots and certify the results.
 A number of choke points can slow down the count, and the most important is the sheer number of mail ballots that county registrars must process after Election Day. California already has far more registered voters than any other state—23 million—and sending mail ballots to every voter creates a processing challenge unlike anywhere else. The Friday after the fall 2024 election, there were still 5.5 million ballots to count, including almost a million in Los Angeles County, almost half a million in San Diego County, and about 460,000 in Alameda County.
 To guard against voter fraud, each ballot’s signature is compared against the registration record on file. When a signature doesn’t match, the ballot enters the “curing” process: the voter is contacted and given an opportunity to sign again. Almost every state has a curing process, but California’s is especially generous, with a deadline significantly later than in any other state.
 The 7-day post-election deadline for receiving ballots also adds some delay. However, among the ballots still to be counted after Election Day, roughly ten times as many arrive by Election Day as after it.
 Several policies can also delay select ballots. Unregistered but voting-eligible California residents can show up on Election Day (or before at an early voting site) to both register and vote. These “conditional registration” ballots go through a separate verification process. Voters showing up at the wrong voting site can cast a “provisional” ballot for any races or measures they are qualified to vote for on the ballot at that site. And if a voter returns a mail ballot to the wrong county registrar, that registrar will mail the ballot to the correct one.
 All these policies stem from a desire to increase access and count every legitimate vote. But they can still overwhelm registrars, who must do the best they can to meet these demands in a timely manner. The state did allocate $29 million to registrars this cycle to help speed things up. But the most important process improvements require significant expenditures like machines and space, and it is unclear whether the appropriated funds are enough to help registrars over the hump. Other changes might accelerate the process, including earlier curing and certification deadlines, but counties would see greater improvements by adding more equipment, space, and staff.
 There is also an important lesson here for consuming news about California’s count. Most races will be decided quickly, but the handful that are close may take quite some time to be called and should not be prejudged based on early returns.
 Likewise, calculations of voter turnout are always low and enormously misleading until the state releases its first “unprocessed ballot count” several days after Election Day. This key report gives an estimate of the number of ballots that remain to be counted as a consequence of the various programs described above. Until that report, thoughtful analysis should refrain from making any conclusions about the quality of voter engagement in the election.
